n: Trust and Company Service Provider Misuse
ds: Misuse of trust and company service providers, including formation agents and nominee or registered-office services, to create, administer or obscure companies and trusts used for laundering. TCSPs may be witting, negligent or exploited.

src.t: FATF and Egmont Group, Concealment of Beneficial Ownership (2018)
FATF, Guidance for a Risk-Based Approach for Trust and Company Service Providers (2019)
FATF, Money Laundering Using Trust and Company Service Providers (2010)

rat: Formation agents and nominee/registered-office providers introduce non-face-to-face clients and sometimes operate client bank accounts.

ind.n: Bulk company formation for undisclosed clients
ind.cx: TCSP forms large numbers of entities with little client information.
ind.ds: TCSP forms large numbers of entities with little client information.

ind.n: Nominee services without disclosure of principal
ind.cx: Nominee directors or shareholders with no record of beneficial owner.
ind.ds: Registered directors or shareholders appear to act for undisclosed principals, serve many entities or have no real decision-making role.

ind.n: Introduced customers with no direct contact
ind.cx: Client business introduced through TCSP with no face-to-face contact and little data.
ind.ds: Client business introduced through TCSP with no face-to-face contact and little data.
Multiple tiers of entities, trusts or foundations, often across secrecy or low-transparency jurisdictions, with no evident business or tax reason.
ind.cn: Complex layered structure without commercial rationale

ind.n: Registered address or mailbox shared by many entities
ind.cx: Same address serves numerous unrelated entities.
ind.ds: Customer shares a registered address, mailbox, agent or phone with numerous unrelated companies, such as a mass-registration or virtual office.
ind.cn: Registered address shared by many entities

ind.n: Frequent changes of directors, names or owners
ind.ds: Customer or entity repeatedly changes name, address, contact details, directors, signatories or ownership.
ind.cn: Frequent changes of customer or entity details

ind.n: Bank accounts opened or operated by TCSP staff
ind.cx: TCSP is signatory or conduit for client funds.
ind.ds: TCSP is signatory or conduit for client funds.

ind.n: Reluctance to provide beneficial owner information
ind.cx: TCSP resists or delays beneficial ownership details.
ind.ds: Customer or intermediary is vague, delayed or inconsistent when asked who owns, controls or ultimately benefits from an account, entity or funds.
ind.cn: Reluctance to disclose beneficial ownership or control

ind.n: Activity in secrecy jurisdictions without links
ind.cx: Entity uses secrecy jurisdictions unrelated to operations.
ind.ds: Entities, accounts or assets are booked in jurisdictions offering strong secrecy or limited transparency, including where unrelated to the entity's operations.

ctl.n: Duplicate and synthetic identity checks at onboarding
ctl.ds: Compares new applicant identifiers such as name, email, phone, address, device and bank account with existing customers, previously declined or exited applicants and known-bad data. Matches are blocked or referred, limiting repeat applicants, synthetic identities and mule recruitment.

ctl.n: Gatekeeper and company service provider due diligence
ctl.ds: Assesses licensing, CDD standards and client mix of formation agents, lawyers and similar professionals and monitors formation volumes and concentration. It targets professional enablers.
Clusters customers, vendors and entities that share addresses, phones, devices, officers or bank details, including against staff records. It reveals common control and hidden relationships.

Identifies the natural persons who ultimately own or control a legal entity or arrangement and verifies them using independent registers and documents, looking through intermediate layers. It is the core defence against anonymity achieved through layered or opaque structures.

Prevents account opening or activity until ownership and control information is provided and verified, with refusals escalated to compliance and unresolved cases handled under a defined policy. It stops relationships starting on withheld or unresolved ownership.

Requires nominee shareholders, directors and signatories to declare their status and name the person they act for, and declines or immobilises bearer instruments. It limits the use of nominees and bearer forms to conceal the real controller.

Assesses introducers and third parties on whom customer due diligence is relied, covering regulation, data access and file quality, backed by written agreements, per-introducer quality reporting and sample testing. It keeps outsourced onboarding to the institution's own standard.
Verifies instructions, detail changes and unusual requests by contacting the customer on a channel held on file, never one supplied in the request. It defeats impersonation and account takeover.

Requires a documented commercial or legal reason for each layer of a multi-tier or cross-border structure, with specialist review and sign-off before approval. Unexplained complexity is treated as a risk driver and can lead to decline.

Tests whether an entity has real operations such as premises, staff, stock and contracts through documents, site or virtual visits, open-source footprint and shell-risk indicators. It helps identify shell and front companies with no genuine activity.

Reviews and updates customer information on a risk-based cycle and when triggers occur, such as ownership change, key attribute change, adverse information or out-of-profile activity. Fresh data keeps risk ratings and expected-activity baselines current.

Secures contractual rights to underlying client information for intermediated or pooled accounts, requires look-through on request and monitors pooled flows against expected activity. It gives visibility of who is really transacting behind an aggregate account.

Identifies and verifies everyone holding signing, control or power-of-attorney rights over an account, and periodically reviews whether those powers remain justified. It reveals third parties who control accounts on behalf of others.

ctl.n: Account restriction, decline and exit policy
ctl.ds: Defines when a relationship or supplier must be declined, restricted or terminated, for example for unresolved due diligence, non-cooperation or unmanageable risk, with timelines and approvers. It prevents indefinite continuation of relationships that cannot be controlled.

Applies enhanced review, approval, limits and conditions to relationships or flows that involve jurisdictions rated higher risk for secrecy, corruption, conflict or weak controls. Triggers include nationality, residence, counterparties and payment routing.

ctl.n: Purpose and intended nature of relationship
ctl.ds: Captures and challenges the stated purpose of the account, expected activity, volumes and geographies at onboarding, creating a baseline against which later behaviour is judged. Vague or implausible answers prompt further enquiry or decline.
